{"id": "43:23/q16", "question": "Does the ancestral claim provide a sound basis for belief?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "43:23/q16/p1", "position": "No; it is blind imitation without independent proof, and inherited belief must be tested by rational or revealed evidence.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhshari says the opponents have no revealed proof and only cite their fathers. Al-Tabrisi argues that rival inherited beliefs conflict while each group rejects the others, so reason or revelation is needed. Al-Qurtubi says they ignored the Messenger's call; al-Baydawi says earlier elites also lacked considered evidence. Al-Bursawi says the ancestors themselves had no independent foundation; al-Alusi says their predecessors had no considered proof. Islahi requires evidence from revelation, reason, or human nature and warns of earlier deniers' fate. The Study Quran says the disbelievers treat ancestry as sufficient justification; al-Tabari calls it a pretext for false religion."}]}
{"id": "43:23/q17", "question": "What broader lesson about worldly comfort and the afterlife is drawn from this conduct?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "43:23/q17/p1", "position": "Attachment to worldly pleasure breeds evil and neglected duties; wisdom seeks God and the afterlife through lasting works.", "reasons": "Al-Razi says worldly life and bodily pleasure underlie evil, whereas love of God and the afterlife underlies good; he quotes a Prophetic saying that love of this world is the root of every sin. Al-Bursawi reports a hadith condemning honor for the affluent over worshippers, selective following of the Quran, and striving for decreed worldly gains rather than earned reward and lasting works. He also reports an aphorism: God guarantees worldly life but commands pursuit of the afterlife, so the wise follow the guided and build the next life with certainty."}]}
{"id": "43:23/q18", "question": "How is the speaker's reply in the following exchange read?", "turns_on": "Whether the reply is narrated as the warner's speech or commanded to him by God.", "positions": [{"id": "43:23/q18/p1", "position": "Ibn Amir and Hafs read 'he said,' making the warner address the people.", "reasons": "Al-Tabrisi reports the reading and Abu Ali's explanation of its speaker."}, {"id": "43:23/q18/p2", "position": "The other readers read 'say,' making God instruct the warner through revelation.", "reasons": "Al-Tabrisi reports the reading and Abu Ali's explanation of its speaker."}]}

{"id": "43:23/q20", "question": "How does the verse serve the surah's larger theme?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "43:23/q20/p1", "position": "It challenges the Makkan idolaters' use of ancestral tradition as a measure of truth within a unified reply to their worldview and objections.", "reasons": "The Study Quran calls the mistaken use of ancestral tradition a major theme and says the surah answers Makkan objections and forms of disbelief. {"id": "43:43/q01", "question": "How does the command follow the preceding warnings about the rejecters?", "turns_on": "Which feature of the preceding passage supplies the immediate rationale: the uncertain timing of punishment, the Prophet's distress at rejection, or the whole argument for revelation.", "positions": [{"id": "43:43/q01/p1", "position": "The Prophet should hold fast regardless of when or how God deals with the rejecters.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān links it to the alternatives of the Prophet's death or witnessing punishment. Al-Biqāʿī says these leave fear and hope, with unseen outcomes and harm and benefit in God's hands. Bursawī says enemies may be punished during or after the Prophet's life, through him at Badr or without him under Abū Bakr; the uncertainty reserves knowledge of the unseen to God. He cites Jāmī's Persian warning against demanding foreknowledge and says to keep the Qurʾān's rulings whether the outcome comes now or in the afterlife. Al-Ālūsī takes the fāʾ as answering an implied condition: since one of the two outcomes must occur, hold fast. Iṣlāḥī says God may judge opponents but grants respite by His established practice. Kur'an Yolu says God will repay all and cannot be resisted."}, {"id": "43:43/q01/p2", "position": "The command steadies the Prophet amid rejection and assures him that his mission remains sound.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī mentions deniers, yet says the Qurʾān leads him to God, divine approval, and reward. Ibn ʿĀshūr connects it to easing distress at unbelief and promising victory; the Prophet must not lose resolve. Iṣlāḥī traces rebellion to affluence and Satan's blinding influence, says the opponents have no argument and will be defeated, and says the Prophet must persist in preaching the religion all prophets confirm. Kur'an Yolu says conditioning can block hearing, sight, and thought, making persuasion hard; preachers should be patient rather than despair at rejection or delayed punishment."}, {"id": "43:43/q01/p3", "position": "The command follows the passage's accumulated case for revelation and the certainty of judgment.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says revelation and prophethood are God's established way, the Book is true, the Prophet a clear messenger, the Godfearing respond, and rejection meets punishment. The preceding material therefore warrants holding fast to the straight path."}]}
{"id": "43:43/q02", "question": "What does holding fast to the revelation require here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "43:43/q02/p1", "position": "Continue to cling firmly to revelation and put it into practice, including its commands and prohibitions.", "reasons": "Muqātil, al-Thaʿlabī, al-Baghawī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Nasafī, Ibn Kathīr, and Study Quran speak of firm adherence to the Qurʾān. Al-Ṭabarī adds its commands; al-Dāmghānī and Ibn al-Jawzī classify this use as action upon revelation. Al-Ṭabrisī specifies proper recitation, obedience, and avoiding prohibitions. Al-Bayḍāwī specifies revealed verses and laws. Al-Qushayrī adds striving without falling short, trust without slackening, stopping at commands, and confidence in the path. Al-Biqāʿī extends diligence from the start of prophethood to dealings with opponents and everything else. Bursawī specifies observing rulings despite delayed outcomes. Al-Ālūsī says the direction may address the Prophet or his community. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the augmented letters in istimsāk intensify holding tightly. Iṣlāḥī applies persistence to preaching monotheism and the Book; Study Quran compares the straight path of 1:6."}]}
{"id": "43:43/q03", "question": "What range of meanings and related forms of the root m-s-k is cited?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "43:43/q03/p1", "position": "The root denotes holding or restraint and takes several contextual senses and related noun forms.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī defines imsāk as restraint, the opposite of release, and also stinginess. He distinguishes mask (leather), misk (perfume), and masaka (bracelets of dhabal, an ivory-like material). Reported exegetes use it for marital retention or taking a wife back (2:229; 65:2), confinement in houses (4:15), stinginess from fear of spending (17:100), preserving the heavens or birds (22:65; 35:41; 67:19), withholding mercy (35:2; 39:38), and grasping a firm handhold (2:256). These are contextual usages rather than rival meanings assigned to this verse."}]}
{"id": "43:43/q04", "question": "Why command the Prophet to hold fast when he already does so?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "43:43/q04/p1", "position": "It commands continued steadfastness and teaches the community to make the same effort.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says an imperative can require persistence in an existing state; he compares Arabic prayers to remain honored and the prayer for guidance in 1:6.
